questions.story:
The Chemical History of a Candle
Adapted from a lecture by Michael Faraday

Passage 1
I propose, in return for the honour you do us by coming to see what we are about, to bring before you a candle. There is not a law under which any part of this universe is governed which does not come into play here. Indeed, there is no better door by which you may enter upon the study of natural philosophy than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle.

Passage 2
Observe the cup that forms at the top of a burning candle. The wax melts, yet it does not run over the edge. Why? Because the current of hot air rising from the flame cools the outer rim, and consequently the wax there remains solid. Nature has thus made, without any assistance from us, a vessel exactly suited to hold the fuel until it is wanted.

Passage 3
Now, a candle does not burn wax. Nothing solid ever burns. The wax is drawn up the wick by capillary attraction, is there converted into a vapour, and it is the vapour, and the vapour only, which takes fire. Blow out the flame and watch the thin column of smoke. Apply a light to the top of that column, however, and the flame will run down it to the wick again.

Passage 4
You may perhaps regard these as small matters, scarcely worth an evening. But I would have you consider that the greatest results are often obtained by the most inconspicuous means. A beautiful thing is always more beautiful when we understand it, and the philosophy of a candle is not made contemptible by the fact that a candle costs a penny.

Passage 5
Here is a jar of the air which has passed through the flame. Lower a lighted taper into it. You observe that it is at once extinguished. Therefore the candle has taken something out of that air and put something else into it. This is the very exchange that occurs in your own lungs at every breath you draw.

Passage 6
I have now to wish you a happy new year, and I hope that, as long as you live, you may be judged as the candle is judged: that you may justify the beauty of your actions by your usefulness to your fellow men. Nothing more than that is required of any of us, and nothing less will serve.
